title: Shoshanat Yaakov
description: Shoshanat Yaakov ("The rose of Jacob"), the Purim song sung after the reading of the Megillah, in Hebrew to an old synagogue tune as Abraham Baer printed it, for 2 to 4 singers. Jacob's rose rejoiced when they saw Mordechai in royal blue; Hashem has been their salvation and their hope in every generation, and none who trust in Him are put to shame. Sung twice, then softly its last line: Charvona too is remembered for good.

credits.tune: synagogue tune, as Abraham Baer printed it (after 1883)

licence.words: public domain: traditional Hebrew liturgy for Purim
licence.tune: public domain: printed by Abraham Baer (died 1894) after 1883 without a mark, which by his 1877 key means a very old, widely sung tune (the older cantors' tunes on the same page are marked "A. W."); not among the pieces his 1883 preface lists as his own; maker unknown
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella (the print is a solo melody)
licence.source: melody from Abraham Baer, Baal T'fillah oder Der practische Vorbeter, 3rd edition (Frankfurt am Main: J. Kauffmann, after 1883), No. 197, "Schoschannas Jakow", p. 59, Solo, Andantino, 4/4, two flats in the signature, in B-flat major (it ends on B-flat), with its quiet last line ("Leise weiter: W'gam charwonoh sochur latow") after a double bar; written here in B-flat as printed. In bars 10 and 11 the print adds a second voice a third above the tune (lo yikalmu lanetzach, kol hachosim bach); the tune is taken as the lower line, which continues the melody by step and ends on the keynote, and the upper notes are used only to check the chords. Baer's triplet groups (dotted eighth, sixteenth, eighth under a 3, and eighth, dotted eighth, sixteenth) are kept, each a beat long. The tune dips to B-flat 3 and C4 under the soprano range for an eighth or a sixteenth at a time, as printed. The words are the print's, respelled from its Ashkenazi transliteration ("Schoschannas jaakow zohaloh w'somechoh") in modern Israeli pronunciation, syllable for syllable as the notes carry them ("v'tik-", "l'ho-" where the print gives the shva no note of its own). Sung twice, then the last line once. The rests the print gives between lines are the breaths; the tempo (60) keeps the shortest syllables a beginner can say. Read from the scan at archive.org/details/der-practische-vorbeter-baer (leaf n103).
